book_so_far:
Ch 1: Ruth cuts clones methodically while training a new employee, Wyatt, avoiding the unopened county permit application on her kitchen table. When she finally reads it Thursday evening, the eleven-page compliance checklist reveals her entire operation—meticulously built over forty years—violates multiple structural, water rights, and tracking requirements. She now has concrete knowledge of the legal gap between what she has built and what the law permits.
Ch 2: Ruth drives to the Planning and Building Department in Eureka on Friday morning to get specific numbers on compliance costs. She learns reinspection and plan review fees, discovers her application cannot be processed until she submits an engineered remediation plan (pushing the 14-18 week inspection queue back further), and overhears county staff discussing how they prioritize consultant-prepared complete applications over incomplete ones—a realization that ground surrendered will have no legal claim waiting.
Ch 3: Saturday morning, Ruth teaches Wyatt the correct topping technique and discovers an opportunity to share an advanced pruning method she has kept secret for forty years, never teaching it to anyone. By mid-July, Ruth transitions from guarding her knowledge to freely teaching, recognizing that this decision reflects her having started to contemplate who will carry the work forward after she is gone.
Ch 4: Corinne Yee from Canopy conducts a site assessment with rangefinder and tablet, measuring four specific violations: the generator shed (38 ft vs 50 ft required from boundary), the intake dam (74 ft vs 100 ft required from watercourse), undocumented irrigation, and unpermittable full-sun area (17,400 sq ft). Corinne offers $9,500/acre for raw parcel or $14,000/acre if Ruth's application is active at closing, with Canopy covering all corrective work. Ruth receives the formal report at 4:52pm, recognizing that the measurements have made her decades of careful placement into quantified noncompliance.
Ch 5: Ruth discovers her forty-year water diversion is unregistered and undocumented. Consulting water rights specialist Deb Ostrander, she learns compliance will require expensive engineering, tankage, and permit processes spanning months to years—with risk of denial for Class II watercourse appropriations. Learning from neighbor Hollis Meeker that Canopy secured water approval for three spring-purchased parcels in six weeks by hiring professional staff, Ruth recognizes the county system as functioning as designed to transfer land from independent growers to corporate buyers.
Ch 6: Ruth calculates the economic value of forty years of labor against Canopy's $812,000 offer ($14,000/acre for 58 acres), discovering approximately $6.77/hour—far below minimum wage. She realizes the money prices the land but cannot price the craft and knowledge living only in her hands and Wyatt's if she continues teaching him. The offer, valid through month's end, becomes a weight she can no longer ignore.
Ch 7: Ruth trains Wyatt on trellis tucking in the south block, showcasing his growing competence until Wyatt mentions offhand a Canopy job posting in Willow Creek for $22/hour with dental and retirement benefits. Ruth recognizes she had unconsciously built a ten-year succession fantasy around him that he never promised, and by end of July quietly recalibrates to teaching him as a temporary worker rather than an heir, without confrontation.
Ch 8: Ruth visits neighboring grower Denny Calloway and discovers he has already sold to Canopy. Denny explains his decision to accept the $14,000/acre buyout rather than fight the permit violations, arguing that legalization is 'just prohibition wearing a tie.' Ruth returns home unable to refute his logic but uncertain whether his acceptance reflects wisdom or resignation.
Ch 9: Ruth works through the permit checklist, completing two items: the irrigation as-built survey and removal of unpermittable full-sun canopy plants. The remaining items—generator shed relocation and intake dam remediation—require engineering estimates beyond her reach, with the dam alone costing $171,000 (nearly three years of her best annual income, $58,000 in 2019). She realizes the numbers will make her decision for her; the county doesn't need to deny the application.
Ch 10: Ruth's daughter Iris visits in early August and explicitly rejects any claim to the farm or inherited knowledge. Ruth accepts that her unspoken hope for succession—first with Wyatt, now with Iris—will not materialize, and recognizes herself as the last person alive who possesses the complete body of knowledge from seed to cure.
Ch 11: Ruth experiences an unexpected heavy rainstorm in early August and spends the night preventing botrytis damage to her crop using a technique learned from Alta Furse in 1998, working alone while Wyatt is away. By morning the vulnerable plants survive intact, but the compliance folder on her kitchen table remains unfinished.
Ch 12: Ruth meets with Canopy's acquisitions counsel for a revised offer. The land purchase price remains $14,000/acre, but a new Cultivation Consulting Agreement clause requires her to sign away her proprietary cultivation knowledge (pruning, curing, botrytis management) as documented video and written protocols, becoming Canopy's sole intellectual property. Ruth refuses the consulting agreement, asserting that her forty years of learned techniques—passed to her by Alta Furse in 1998 and now being taught to Wyatt—belong only to her hands and can only be taught to a person, never to a training protocol. She leaves with the land purchase still unsigned.
